---
title: "Glossary"
---

A plain-language reference for the R, tidyverse, workflow, and epidemiology
terms you'll meet in this book. Two kinds of reader should feel at home here:
someone brand new to R who wants a word explained, and an epidemiologist who
knows the statistics cold but not the R name for the thing. Where a SAS
comparison genuinely helps, we make one — but only where it earns its keep.

Definitions are short on purpose. Where a term has a natural home chapter,
there's a "(see …)" link, but every entry is meant to stand on its own.

## A

Adjusted estimate
: An effect (like an odds ratio) that accounts for other variables in the
  model at the same time, so each one is reported holding the others constant.
  In a logistic regression with several predictors, every coefficient is
  already adjusted for the rest.

Aesthetic (`aes()`)
: In ggplot2, the mapping from a column in your data to something you can see
  on the plot — the x position, the y position, color, size, and so on. `aes(x
  = date, y = cases)` says "put date on the x-axis, cases on the y." (see
  [Data visualization](../03-data-visualization/index.qmd))

Aggregate (count) data
: Data where each row is already a summed-up total — cases per town per day,
  say — rather than one row per person. The opposite of a line-list. Most of
  the CT COVID data in this book is aggregate count data.

API (Application Programming Interface)
: A structured way for one program to ask another for data over the internet.
  Instead of downloading a file by hand, you send a request in code and get
  data back. (see [APIs and functions](../apis-functions/index.qmd))

Argument
: A value you hand to a function to tell it what to do. In `read_csv("data.csv")`,
  the string `"data.csv"` is the argument. Functions often take several,
  usually named (`n = 10`).

Arrange (`arrange()`)
: The dplyr verb that sorts rows by one or more columns. `arrange(desc(date))`
  puts the newest dates first. Like an `ORDER BY` in SQL or `PROC SORT`.

Assignment (`<-`)
: How you save a result under a name so you can use it later. `covid <-
  read_csv(...)` reads the file and stores it in an object called `covid`. The
  arrow points from the value into the name.

arrow (the arrow package)
: R's interface to Apache Arrow — a columnar data format plus a query engine
  that reads only the columns and rows a query actually touches. Lets you use
  `dplyr` verbs on files far larger than your computer's memory. (see [When the
  data outgrows your laptop](../big-data/index.qmd))

## B

Branch
: In git, a parallel line of work. You make a branch to try changes without
  touching the main version, then merge it back in when you're happy. (see
  [Version control](../version-control/index.qmd))

broom
: A tidyverse-friendly package that turns messy model output into a tidy
  tibble. `broom::tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE)` gives you one row per term with
  its estimate and confidence interval. (see [Modeling](../data-analysis/modeling.qmd))

## C

`case_when()`
: A dplyr function for building a new column from a cascade of "if this, then
  that" rules — handy for recoding or bucketing a continuous variable into
  categories. Reads a bit like a `SELECT … CASE` or a chain of `IF/ELSE`
  statements.

Case fatality rate (CFR)
: The share of diagnosed cases that end in death — deaths divided by cases. A
  descriptive proportion, not a rate over person-time. (see [Describing and
  testing](../data-analysis/describing-and-testing.qmd))

Chi-square test
: A test for whether two categorical variables are associated — the counts in
  a cross-tab, compared against what you'd expect if there were no
  relationship. `chisq.test()` in R; the CHISQ option on `PROC FREQ` in SAS.

Choropleth
: A map that shades each area (here, each CT town) by a value — case rate,
  count, whatever — so the color tells the story geographically. (see [Data
  visualization](../03-data-visualization/index.qmd))

Code chunk
: A block of runnable R inside a Quarto document, fenced by `` ```{r} `` …
  `` ``` ``. When you render, the code runs and its output lands in the
  finished page.

Commit
: A saved snapshot of your project in git, with a short message describing what
  changed. Your history is the chain of commits. (see [Version
  control](../version-control/index.qmd))

Confidence interval
: A range of plausible values for an estimate. For an odds ratio, if the 95%
  interval crosses 1, the association isn't statistically clear at that level —
  the "no effect" value is still in play.

Count vs. percent
: A raw tally versus that tally as a share of some total. Counts answer "how
  many," percents answer "how much of the whole" — you usually want both, which
  is why `janitor`'s `adorn_` helpers add percents onto a count table.

CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network)
: R's official package repository — the place `pak::pak()` (or the older
  `install.packages()`) downloads from. If a package is "on CRAN," it's been
  through some basic checks and is one command away.

Cross-tabulation
: A table of counts broken down by two categorical variables at once — the epi
  workhorse. `janitor::tabyl(data, var1, var2)` builds one; think `PROC FREQ`
  with two variables. (see [Describing and testing](../data-analysis/describing-and-testing.qmd))

Cumulative vs. incremental
: Cumulative counts are running totals that only ever grow (total cases to
  date); incremental counts are the *new* amount in each period (new cases
  today). You get daily new cases by subtracting each day's cumulative total
  from the one before.

Columnar (column-oriented) format
: A file layout that stores all the values of one column together, instead of
  storing each row's values together the way a CSV does. Reading three columns
  out of forty then costs three columns' worth of disk, and repeated values in
  a column compress extremely well. Parquet is the format you'll meet. (see
  [Parquet](../big-data/parquet.qmd))

Corrected result
: A laboratory result re-sent to replace one already reported, flagged in HL7
  with a result status of `C`. Corrections are why a count you briefed on
  Monday can be different on Friday — deduplicate by keeping the *latest*
  result for a specimen, not the first.

## D

Data frame / tibble
: A rectangular table of data — rows and columns — which is how R holds most
  datasets. A **tibble** is the tidyverse's modern data frame: same idea,
  friendlier printing and fewer surprises. Closest thing to a SAS dataset.

Denominator
: The "out of how many" underneath a rate — the population at risk. Counts
  alone can mislead; a big town has more cases simply because more people live
  there. Age-adjusted rates in particular need a population denominator to be
  meaningful, which is why they wait for a dataset that supplies one.

Descriptive statistics
: The plain summaries — counts, percents, means, ranges — that describe what's
  in your data before any formal test. The R answer to a first pass with `PROC
  MEANS` and `PROC FREQ`. (see [Describing and testing](../data-analysis/describing-and-testing.qmd))

dplyr
: The tidyverse package for manipulating data frames, built around a handful of
  verbs — `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `arrange`, `group_by`, `summarise`.
  The core of most wrangling in this book.

DuckDB
: An analytical database that runs inside your R session — no server, no
  administrator, one file. Reads parquet and CSV directly, speaks SQL, and
  handles the window functions and exact quantiles arrow's engine won't. (see
  [Databases, with DuckDB standing in](../big-data/duckdb.qmd))

`DBI` / `dbplyr`
: The two packages that connect R to a database. `DBI` handles the connection
  and raw SQL; `dbplyr` translates `dplyr` pipelines into SQL so you can query
  a database with verbs you already know. Both work against Postgres, SQL
  Server, DuckDB, and more — change the connection, keep the pipeline.

## E

Endpoint
: The specific URL an API exposes for a particular dataset or action. You point
  your request at an endpoint and it hands back the matching data. (see [APIs
  and functions](../apis-functions/index.qmd))

ELR (Electronic Laboratory Reporting)
: The stream of messages laboratories send to public health with test results,
  usually in the HL7 v2 format, which surveillance systems flatten into one
  very wide table of one row per result. (see [When the data outgrows your
  laptop](../big-data/index.qmd))

## F

Factor
: R's type for a categorical variable, with a fixed set of allowed values
  called levels. Models use the first level as the reference group, so factors
  matter when you fit a logistic regression. Like a SAS variable with a defined
  format for its categories.

Filter (`filter()`)
: The dplyr verb that keeps only the rows matching a condition —
  `filter(town == "Hartford")`. This is subsetting rows, the equivalent of a
  `WHERE` clause or a subsetting `IF` in a SAS DATA step.

Fisher's exact test
: An alternative to the chi-square test used when cell counts are small, where
  the chi-square approximation gets shaky. `fisher.test()` in R; the EXACT
  option on `PROC FREQ`.

Freeze
: A Quarto feature (`freeze: auto`) that caches the output of your code chunks
  so they only re-run when the source changes. It keeps builds fast and results
  stable between renders.

Function
: A named, reusable piece of code that takes inputs (arguments) and returns a
  result. `read_csv()`, `filter()`, and `mean()` are all functions; you can
  also write your own. (see [APIs and functions](../apis-functions/index.qmd))

`fs`
: A tidyverse-adjacent package for working with files and folders — listing,
  checking existence, creating directories — with consistent, predictable
  behavior across operating systems.

## G

Geom
: A ggplot2 layer that decides *how* your mapped data is drawn — points
  (`geom_point()`), lines (`geom_line()`), bars, and so on. You stack geoms to
  build a plot up in layers.

ggplot2
: The tidyverse plotting package, built on the "grammar of graphics": you
  describe a plot as data plus aesthetic mappings plus geoms, and add pieces
  with `+`. (see [Data visualization](../03-data-visualization/index.qmd))

git
: The version-control system that tracks changes to your files over time, so
  you can see history, undo mistakes, and collaborate. GitHub is a website that
  hosts git projects. (see [Version control](../version-control/index.qmd))

glue
: A stringr-adjacent package for building strings by dropping R values straight
  into `{braces}` inside text — great for one-line summaries like "Hartford
  reported {n} new cases."

`group_by()` / `summarise()`
: The dplyr pair for split-apply-combine: `group_by()` splits the data into
  groups (say, by town), `summarise()` collapses each group to one summary row.
  This is `PROC MEANS`/`PROC SUMMARY` with a `BY` statement, done in a pipe.

## H

`here` (the here package)
: A package that builds file paths from your project's root, so
  `here("data", "raw", "covid.csv")` works no matter where your script runs.
  It's the reliable alternative to hard-coded or fragile relative paths.

httr2
: The package this book uses to talk to web APIs — you build a request piece by
  piece, send it, and pull data out of the response. (see [APIs and
  functions](../apis-functions/index.qmd))

## J

janitor
: A package for cleaning up real-world data: `clean_names()` fixes ugly column
  names in one shot, and `tabyl()` plus the `adorn_` helpers build tidy count
  tables with totals and percents. (see [Cleaning data](../02-cleaning-data/index.qmd))

Join (merge)
: Combining two tables by matching on a shared key column. `left_join()` keeps
  every row on the left and pulls in matches from the right; `inner_join()`
  keeps only matches; there are also `right_`, `full_`, `semi_`, and
  `anti_join()`. This is a SQL join or a SAS `MERGE`. (see [Joins](../further-reading/joins.qmd))

## L

Lazy evaluation
: Building up a query without running it, then executing the whole thing at
  once at the end. `dplyr` verbs on an arrow dataset or a database table record
  what you asked for; `collect()` is what actually runs it and brings the
  result back into R. Putting `collect()` last is the whole point. (see [When
  the data outgrows your laptop](../big-data/index.qmd))

LOINC
: The standard code system for *what test was performed* — `94500-6` is
  "SARS-CoV-2 RNA by NAA with probe detection." Pairs with SNOMED CT, which
  codes the answer.

Library
: The command `library(dplyr)` loads an installed package so you can use its
  functions in the current session. Heads up for SAS users: this is *not* a SAS
  library — in R a package is code, not a folder of datasets.

Line-list
: Data with one row per person or event, carrying individual-level detail — the
  opposite of aggregate count data. The book uses a synthetic line-list to
  demonstrate analyses that need person-level records.

Logistic regression
: A model for a yes/no outcome (died vs. survived) that reports effects as odds
  ratios. Fit with `glm(..., family = "binomial")` in base R, or the
  tidymodels way; the SAS equivalent is `PROC LOGISTIC`. (see [Modeling](../data-analysis/modeling.qmd))

lubridate
: The tidyverse package for working with dates and times — parsing text into
  real dates with `as_date()`, doing date arithmetic, pulling out the week or
  month. Sidesteps the classic Excel date-serial-number headaches.

## M

Merge (git)
: In git, combining the changes from one branch into another. Distinct from a
  data join, which merges *tables* — same word, different world. (see [Version
  control](../version-control/index.qmd))

Missing value (`NA`)
: R's marker for "no value here." `NA` is contagious in arithmetic (anything
  plus `NA` is `NA`), so you handle it deliberately with tools like `drop_na()`
  and `replace_na()`. Roughly R's version of a SAS missing (`.`).

Mutate (`mutate()`)
: The dplyr verb that adds or changes a column — `mutate(rate = cases /
  population)`. It's how you compute new variables, like an assignment inside a
  SAS DATA step.

## O

Odds ratio
: The measure of association a logistic regression reports: how the odds of the
  outcome change with a predictor. An odds ratio of 1 means no association, and
  it is *not* the same as a risk ratio — the book is careful about that. (see
  [Modeling](../data-analysis/modeling.qmd))

Open Data Portal
: A public website that publishes government datasets for anyone to download or
  query, often through an API. Connecticut's COVID data lives on one. (see
  [APIs and functions](../apis-functions/index.qmd))

OLTP / OLAP
: Two jobs a database can be built for. **OLTP** (transaction processing —
  Postgres, SQL Server) handles many small reads and writes touching a few
  rows: the system of record your agency runs on. **OLAP** (analytical
  processing — DuckDB) handles a few enormous scans producing one summary
  table: what your analysis does. It's why the DBA won't let you run a
  sixteen-million-row scan against production.

## P

Package
: A bundle of ready-made R code (functions, data, docs) you install once and
  load when you need it. The tidyverse is a family of packages designed to work
  together.

`pak` (the pak package)
: The modern package installer this book uses. You bootstrap it once with
  `install.packages("pak")`, then install everything else with `pak::pak("dplyr")`
  — one command that pulls from CRAN, GitHub, or Bioconductor, resolves
  dependencies cleanly, and downloads in parallel. Replaces the older
  `install.packages()` for day-to-day use. (see [Orientation](../00-orientation/index.qmd))

Parquet
: A columnar, compressed, binary file format that stores its own column types
  and statistics. Typically several times smaller than the equivalent CSV,
  much faster to query, readable by R, Python, DuckDB, Spark, and every major
  cloud warehouse. (see [Parquet](../big-data/parquet.qmd))

Partitioning
: Splitting a dataset across folders named for a column's value —
  `collection_year=2021/collection_month=1/` — so a query filtered on that
  column never opens the other folders. Partition on what you filter on, and
  not on anything with thousands of distinct values. (see
  [Parquet](../big-data/parquet.qmd))

Predicate pushdown
: Letting the storage layer do the filtering. Because a parquet file records
  the minimum and maximum of every column in every chunk, an engine can skip
  whole chunks that can't possibly match your `filter()` without reading them.

Pipe (`|>`)
: The operator that passes the result of one step into the next as its first
  argument, so you can read code left-to-right, top-to-bottom:
  `covid |> filter(...) |> summarise(...)`. It's what makes tidyverse code read
  like a recipe.

p-value
: The probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if there were truly
  no association. Small p-values flag "probably not chance" — but a tiny
  p-value is not the same as a big or important effect.

Project
: A self-contained working folder that RStudio or Positron treats as home base,
  keeping your data, scripts, and outputs together. Opening the project sets
  everything up so paths and packages behave. (see [Orientation](../00-orientation/index.qmd))

## Q

Quarto
: The publishing system this book is written in. A Quarto document mixes prose
  with runnable code chunks and renders to HTML, PDF, and more — so the analysis
  and the write-up live in one file.

## R

recode
: Replacing the values in a column with new ones — turning `1`/`2` into
  `"case"`/`"control"`, for instance. Often done with `case_when()` or dplyr's
  recoding helpers.

Relative path
: A file location written relative to some starting point rather than from the
  root of the disk. Fragile relative paths break when scripts move, which is
  exactly the problem `here()` solves.

renv
: A package that records the exact versions of every package your project uses,
  so a collaborator (or future you) can restore the same setup with
  `renv::restore()`. A cornerstone of reproducibility.

Reproducibility
: The property that someone else can re-run your work and get the same result —
  the point of projects, `here()`, renv, seeds, and Quarto freeze all working
  together. The book treats it as a spectrum, not a pass/fail.

polars
: A Python dataframe library built on the same columnar, lazy,
  query-optimized ideas as arrow — worth knowing about because it reads the
  same parquet files you write, with your types intact. The format is the
  handoff between languages, not a CSV. (see [Databases, with DuckDB standing
  in](../big-data/duckdb.qmd))

## S

Seed (`set.seed()`)
: A number that fixes R's random-number generator so "random" operations come
  out the same every time you run them. Set a seed before anything random and
  your results reproduce exactly.

Select (`select()`)
: The dplyr verb that keeps, drops, or reorders *columns* — `select(town, date,
  cases)`. Column-side counterpart to `filter()`; like `KEEP`/`DROP` in SAS.

`sf` (simple features)
: The R package for spatial data — it holds map geometries (town boundaries) in
  a data frame you can wrangle with dplyr and plot with ggplot2. (see [Data
  visualization](../03-data-visualization/index.qmd))

Snapshot
: A dataset saved at a fixed point in time. Because open data updates and gets
  revised, the book pins to a snapshot so the numbers stay stable as you code
  along.

SODA (Socrata Open Data API)
: The particular API standard the Connecticut open-data portal uses. It lets you
  query for just the rows and columns you want instead of downloading
  everything. (see [APIs and functions](../apis-functions/index.qmd))

String
: Text data, written in quotes: `"Hartford"`. The stringr package gives you
  consistent tools for detecting, replacing, trimming, and reshaping strings.

stringr
: The tidyverse package for working with text — `str_detect()`, `str_replace()`,
  `str_to_title()`, `str_trim()` and friends — used here to guard and tidy up
  messy town names.

Summarise (`summarise()`)
: See **group_by / summarise** — the dplyr verb that collapses rows into summary
  values like counts and means, usually one row per group.

Synthetic data
: Fake data generated to look realistic without being anyone's real records.
  The book uses a synthetic line-list so it can teach person-level analysis
  without exposing real individuals. (see [Building a dataset](../building-a-dataset/index.qmd))

SNOMED CT
: The standard clinical vocabulary used for *the answer* a test returned —
  `260373001` is "Detected", `260415000` is "Not detected". Codes like these
  are identifiers, not numbers: read them as text or you will eventually lose
  a leading zero.

SQL
: The language databases speak. You don't have to write it to use a database
  from R — `dbplyr` translates `dplyr` for you — but `show_query()` will show
  you the SQL it generated, which is the least painful way to learn it.

## T

`tabyl`
: janitor's tabulation function — a tidy, pipeable frequency or cross-tab table,
  dressed up with the `adorn_` helpers for totals and percents. The everyday
  stand-in for `PROC FREQ`. (see [Describing and testing](../data-analysis/describing-and-testing.qmd))

tidy data
: Data arranged so each variable is a column, each observation a row, and each
  cell one value. Tidyverse tools expect this shape, and getting there is half
  the battle of a clean analysis.

tidymodels
: A family of packages (parsnip, recipes, workflows, broom) that brings the
  tidyverse's consistent style to modeling — a recipe declares preprocessing, a
  parsnip spec picks the model, and a workflow bundles them to fit. (see
  [Modeling](../data-analysis/modeling.qmd))

tidyr
: The tidyverse package for reshaping data — `pivot_longer()`/`pivot_wider()` to
  go between wide and long, plus `separate()`, `unite()`, and `uncount()`.

tidyverse
: The curated collection of R packages (dplyr, readr, ggplot2, tidyr, stringr,
  and more) that share a common design and are meant to work smoothly together.
  This book teaches the tidyverse first and skips base R.

Trend in proportions
: A test for whether a proportion moves steadily in one direction across an
  ordered variable — rising case-positivity over time, say. `prop.trend.test()`
  in R. (see [Describing and testing](../data-analysis/describing-and-testing.qmd))

Turnaround time
: The gap between specimen collection and the result being reported. It
  stretches when laboratories are busiest, which means the most recent days in
  any surveillance count are the least complete — the usual reason a number
  keeps rising after it was briefed. (see [Answering the lab-feed
  questions](../big-data/project.qmd))

## U

`uncount()`
: A tidyr function that expands a count table back into one row per unit — the
  reverse of tallying. Handy for turning aggregate counts into a line-list-shaped
  table when an analysis needs individual rows.

## V

Vector
: R's most basic data structure: an ordered sequence of values, all the same
  type (a column of a data frame is a vector). Most R functions operate on whole
  vectors at once rather than looping row by row.

View (database)
: A saved query that behaves like a table. `CREATE VIEW lab_results AS SELECT
  * FROM read_parquet(...)` lets you query a folder of parquet files by name
  without importing anything — the database stores the definition, the files
  stay the data.

## W

Window function
: A calculation that runs across a set of rows related to the current one
  without collapsing them — ranking each specimen's results by date to keep
  the latest, or a running total. Standard in SQL, absent from arrow's engine,
  which is a common reason to reach for DuckDB.

Wide vs. long
: Two shapes for the same data. Wide spreads a variable across many columns (one
  column per week); long stacks it into fewer columns with more rows (a week
  column and a value column). `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()` move between
  them — this is `PROC TRANSPOSE`'s job in SAS.

Working directory
: The folder R currently treats as "here" when it reads or writes files. Rather
  than fiddling with it, this book leans on projects and `here()` so paths just
  work.
